Systematic Review Finds Multi-Disease Artificial Intelligence Lacks Prospective Clinical Trial Evidence

Multimorbidity currently affects more than 37 percent of the global adult population and accounts for 55 to 80 percent of healthcare spending in high-income systems, yet diagnostic artificial intelligence systems remain overwhelmingly restricted to single conditions. According to a systematic review published in Frontiers in Digital Health, this narrow design creates a profound structural mismatch with the multi-disease complexity encountered in real-world clinical practice. Researchers evaluated advanced computing technologies designed for simultaneous multi-domain disease detection and prediction across twelve disease groups mapped to the World Health Organization International Classification of Diseases eleventh revision chapters. While models demonstrated high discrimination, the investigation identified substantial gaps separating current algorithms from safe clinical deployment.

The systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered with the Open Science Framework under registration digital object identifier 10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45 on 25 October 2026. The authors systematically searched nine major electronic databases—PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Springer Link, Wiley, MDPI, and Google Scholar—for peer-reviewed literature published between January 2015 and 31 August 2026. Utilizing database-specific Boolean search strings combining artificial intelligence terminology with terms for the twelve review-defined disease groups, the team initially identified 4,215 records. Following the removal of 847 duplicate entries, 3,368 records remained for preliminary screening. Assessing 612 full-text articles resulted in the exclusion of 332 studies, leaving 280 studies that met the eligibility criteria for qualitative synthesis.

Methodological quality across the reviewed literature was formally appraised using the QUADAS-2 and PROBAST assessment tools, with study screening agreement measured at a Cohen’s kappa of 0.84. Among the 280 included papers, 185 provided quantitative performance metrics suitable for descriptive, non-pooled synthesis. The investigators highlighted that deep learning architectures—including convolutional neural networks, long short-term memory networks, vision transformers, and graph neural networks—reported high but heterogeneous discrimination, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values ranging between 0.85 and 0.991 across the twelve disease categories. The review authors emphasized that these disparate figures originated from differing classification tasks, varied benchmark datasets, and distinct validation designs, rather than representing pooled estimates or establishing the superiority of any single network architecture.

Within the analyzed literature, three of the highest-reporting single-disease studies illustrated the current diagnostic performance boundaries, though the researchers noted they were retrospective and not directly comparable. These notable benchmarks included a diabetic retinopathy detection system reporting an area under the curve of 0.991 across a sample of 128,175 individuals, a cancer whole-slide image classification model achieving an area under the curve of 0.98 using 44,732 samples, and a cardiac arrhythmia detection algorithm demonstrating an area under the curve of 0.97 across 91,232 electrocardiograms. In terms of technical implementation, convolutional neural networks constituted the most prevalent architecture, utilized in 26 percent of the reviewed studies. Additionally, Python served as the primary programming language across the field, appearing in 68 percent of the included investigations.

Despite these elevated performance metrics, the systematic review uncovered three persistent, systemic deficiencies across the broader research domain. First, the authors identified an acute lack of demographic representation from developing nations and low- and middle-income populations within model training datasets. Second, the literature revealed an extreme scarcity of evidence derived from randomized prospective clinical trials demonstrating measurable improvements in patient outcomes.

Subject of Research: Artificial intelligence technologies for simultaneous multi-domain disease detection and prediction

Article Title: Multiple disease detection and prediction using advanced computing technologies: a comprehensive systematic review

Article References: Choudhary, A. K., Mishra, K. N., Lal, R. K., & Mishra, A. (2026). Multiple disease detection and prediction using advanced computing technologies: a comprehensive systematic review. Frontiers in Digital Health, 8, Article 2020306. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2026.2020306

Keywords: multimorbidity, multiple disease detection, systematic review, deep learning, convolutional neural networks, long short-term memory, vision transformers, graph neural networks, Software as a Medical Device, ICD-11 chapters, PRISMA 2020, QUADAS-2, PROBAST, federated learning, prospective randomized trials, electronic health records
